newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Bad Turkmen harvest points to grain imports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bad Turkmen harvest points to grain imports.

text.p: For the second year in a row, Turkmenistan's hopes of achieving self-sufficiency in grain have been dashed and the Central Asian republic is set to remain a net importer, analysts said on Wednesday.
The former Soviet republic harvested a meagre 600,000 tonnes of grain this year, way below the official target of 1.2 million tonnes, the State Statistics Committee said in a preliminary report.
The figure was only a slight improvement on the disastrous 1996 harvest, which totalled just 480,000 tonnes.
"Turkmenistan is a net importer," said a London-based grains analyst. "It will continue to buy from Kazakhstan, Russia and others."
"Others", a separate source said, may have in the past 12 months included Australia and unnamed suppliers delivering via Pacific outlets.
"We don't have this myth of happy peasants labouring," said one grains source, adding that Turkmenistan imported up to 700,000 tonnes of grain over the 1996/97 marketing year.
With total domestic supply of around 1.1 million tonnes over 1996/97, Turkmen per capita consumption may have been around 200-220 kgs, one of the highest rates in the world.
But the ambitious plans of Turkmenistan's strongman president, Saparmurat Niyazov, to boost annual grain output to two million tonnes annually by 2000 seem unlikely to be realised, analysts said.
"It's business as usual, with them coming up with unrealistic targets," said the grains source.

The harvest is a political embarrassment for Niyazov, who is the focus of a Stalinist-style personality cult and has promised speedy prosperity for the four million population in a "1,000 days" economic programme.

Niyazov reacted to the poor harvest figures in a time-honoured fashion by firing a string of officials, including Agriculture Minister Pirkuli Odeyev and acting Deputy Prime Minister Nurmukhammed Ashirov.

"Good undertakings of peasants have been blocked by the bureaucracy of the authorities," Niyazov thundered on state television on Tuesday. "It's abnormal to gather such poor harvests in the region with fertile lands and irrigation."
But Turkmenistan, bordering northern Iran and Afghanistan, is largely empty, parched desert.
"The climate is marginal," said the London-based analyst, "and the Turkmens don't have a lot of arable land."
Most Soviet-built irrigation canals, feeding off the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to water the republic's cotton crop, are unlined and uncovered, causing valuable water to leak or evaporate.
Niyazov also clings to Soviet-era central planning, with his few cautious steps toward private farming only sowing greater confusion.
Faced with a state procurement price for grain at a low $70-$80 a tonne, many farmers are only willing to labour on market-garden crops which can be turned into cash quickly in the bazaars.
"They've still got to work out their transport," a Western diplomat said.
The grains source said Turkmenistan was eager to avoid the stranglehold that Russia has on rail transport tariffs and to diversify supplies.
Turkmenistan, owed hundreds of millions of dollars for its exports of natural gas to ex-Soviet states, desperately lacks cash to pump into agricultural reform.

Most of its money goes on expensive grain imports -- Niyazov spent $800 million last year to feed the population, whose low salaries have made bread a vital staple and sent per capita consumption levels soaring.
"It's not the Horn of Africa, even though they seem to be on the verge of running out and seem to have no resources," said the grains source. "Somehow they manage to scrape by."
